en_old: In older tumbler locks it was enough to lift the tumbler high enough and the bolt moved. London locksmith Robert Barron changed that with a patent of 31 October 1778. In his lock the bolt jammed if a tumbler was lifted too little, and jammed just the same if it was lifted too much. He also used two tumblers instead of one, each needing a different height. A simple idea, and most later lever locks rest on it. Joseph Bramah later analysed it, both respectfully and critically.

en_old: We call the wooden bolt with dropping pins "Egyptian" because nineteenth-century travellers saw it daily in Cairo, where merchants carried long keys over their shoulders. But did ancient Egyptians use it? In 1883 Augustus Pitt-Rivers found the evidence doubtful: the earliest certain pin key was Roman. Romans cast the same mechanism in bronze, and Pitt-Rivers drew a reconstruction from fragments kept in Mainz. The name stuck, though the trail runs rather through the Near East and Rome.
